comparisons.peer_topic: USPB Expense and Credit Loss Trends
comparisons.peer_summary: USPB expenses decreased 1% to $10 billion due to productivity savings and lower technology costs, while cost of credit increased to $8.6 billion (from $6.7 billion) primarily due to a 45% rise in net credit losses from maturing card vintages and macroeconomic pressures on lower FICO band customers, partially offset by a lower ACL build.
comparisons.comparison: Both Bank of America and Citigroup disclose specific financial drivers impacting their lending and consumer banking operations, but they focus on different metrics. BAC reports on loan origination demand trends (first mortgage originations increasing $1.1 billion and home equity decreasing $878 million due to demand changes). Citigroup, in contrast, reports on the 'cost of credit' and net credit losses for its US Personal Banking (USPB) segment, noting a $1.9 billion increase ($8.6 billion vs $6.7 billion) driven by maturing card vintages and macroeconomic pressures on lower FICO band customers. While both discuss lending-related performance, BAC focuses on volume/demand drivers of originations, whereas C focuses on credit quality/loss drivers of existing book performance.

sentences.text: First mortgage loan originations for Consumer Banking and the total Corporation increased $1.1 billion and $1.7 billion primarily driven by higher demand.
Home equity production in Consumer Banking and the total Corporation decreased $878 million and $930 million primarily driven by lower demand.
Cost of credit increased to $8.6 billion, compared to $6.7 billion in the prior year.

The increase was driven by higher net credit losses (up 45%), primarily reflecting the continued maturation of multiple cards loan vintages originated in recent years, as well as macroeconomic pressures related to the elevated inflationary and interest rate environment impacting both cards portfolios, with lower FICO band customers primarily driving the increase.

comparisons.peer_topic: Average Daily Value at Risk (VaR) 2024 and 2023 Comparison
comparisons.peer_summary: The firm's average daily VaR decreased to $92 million in 2024 from $99 million in 2023, driven primarily by lower volatility and decreased interest rate risk, partially offset by increased equity price exposures and overall exposure levels.
comparisons.comparison: Neither Bank of America nor Goldman Sachs discusses consumer loan originations or home equity production in the provided disclosures. BAC's disclosure focuses on Consumer Banking loan demand drivers. GS's disclosure focuses on firm-wide Value at Risk (VaR) metrics driven by market volatility and interest rate/equity price exposures. There is no substantive common topic regarding consumer lending demand or originations between these specific texts.

comparisons.comparison: Both Bank of America and JPMorgan Chase disclose changes in loan volumes, but for different segments and driven by different factors. BAC reports on Consumer Banking first mortgage and home equity loan originations, attributing a $1.1 billion increase in first mortgages to 'higher demand.' JPMorgan reports on total loans (primarily CIB and AWM) increasing $19.8 billion, and lending-related commitments decreasing $5.3 billion. While both touch upon loan balance/originations, BAC's is specific to consumer mortgage demand, whereas JPM's is a broad aggregate including institutional markets and securities-based lending, with no mention of consumer mortgage demand trends in the cited JPM text.
